note: Logic sound; the drought-means-less-vegetation link is a fair, explicitly flagged common-sense step that the credited answer requires, and B/D/E notes correctly test for a fact that does not vary between periods.
Correct E with the perceived-risk link made explicit; B note correctly separates recorded toll from actual toll; typo fixed, rest of old steps preserved.

steps.label: Given that ...
steps.body: The power plant opened and started discharging wastewater into the river.

steps.label: Why is it that ...
steps.body: Shortly after, anglers downstream caught fewer bass overall?

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.

Think about what "number of bass caught" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:
1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.
2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.

Expect most of the answers we eliminate to come in on road 1, with at least one sneaking in on road 2.

Most students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Eliminate four answers that explain fewer bass caught, by either road. The correct answer will do neither, or it will push the other way: more bass or more fishing, which should mean *more* bass caught.

Be careful with any answer about anglers. It isn't out of scope. Anglers are half the equation.

notes.body: A takes road 1. If the wastewater draws in fish that prey on bass, more bass get eaten and fewer are left downstream to catch. That explains the drop in bass caught, so A is out.
B also takes road 1. The warmer discharge sends bass off to find cooler water elsewhere. Fewer bass stay downstream of the plant, so anglers there catch fewer. That explains the drop, so eliminate B.

C pushes the other way. Better access brings more anglers fishing for bass downstream. More people fishing should mean more bass caught, not fewer, so C cannot explain the decrease.

Could you rescue C by imagining the extra anglers fished the bass out? Only by inventing that story yourself, and it runs against what C actually tells us. C's own effect is more people fishing, and on its face that means more bass caught. The four other answers each point straight at fewer bass caught; C points the other way. That is what marks the answer that does not belong.

D is the road 2 answer, and it is easy to throw out as off topic because it is about anglers, not bass. The bass may be fine. But noise makes that stretch of river a less popular place to fish, and fewer anglers catch fewer bass. That is exactly the decrease described, so D explains it and is out.

E is road 1 again. Turbulence from the wastewater disrupted the river vegetation and destroyed some of the bass's habitat. Less habitat supports fewer bass downstream, so fewer get caught. E explains the drop.

note: C note's closing rule (an answer that needs a supplied step does not explain) was overbroad and clashes with paradox questions that rely on obvious links; replaced with the direction-based reason.

steps.label: Apparent Paradox
steps.body: Jimmy replaced the old gas water heater with a new, pilotless, gas water heater that is rated as highly efficient. After that, Jimmy's gas bills increased.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is less a paradox than a surprise. A highly efficient heater sounds like it should lower the bill. But the bill depends on two things: how much gas the whole household burns, and the price of each unit of gas. The water heater is only one of the things in the house that burns gas.

So the bill can rise, even with a better heater, by two routes.

Route one: more gas used somewhere in the household. More people, a new gas appliance, more heating.

Route two: a higher price for each unit of gas.

The new heater's efficiency only shrinks the heater's own use. It does nothing about the rest of the house or the price.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Eliminate four answers that take one of the two routes: more gas burned in Jimmy's household, or a higher price per unit. The correct answer will do neither. A good place to look: an answer about the water heater itself, since the stimulus already tells us the heater is efficient, which points toward less gas, not more.

notes.body:
A explains nothing. It says the new heater uses a smaller percentage of the household's gas than the old one did. A percentage is a share, not an amount, so A does not tell us whether total gas use went up, or why.

Try numbers. Old heater: 50% of 100 units, so 50 units. New heater at 40%: if the household still uses 100 units, the heater uses 40; if the household now uses 150, the heater uses 60. A fits either story because it only describes how the gas is split. It gives no extra gas use and no higher price, so it is the one answer that does not contribute. Careful: A does not even say the new heater burns less gas than the old one, so it does not deepen the puzzle either. It simply gives no cause.

B is route one. Jimmy's uncle moved in shortly after the installation, doubling the household. Twice as many people means more hot water and more gas burned overall. More gas used raises the bill even with an efficient heater, so B helps explain the increase.

C is route one through a new appliance. Jimmy started using a gas dryer when the heater was replaced. Before that, the laundry was done at a laundromat, so this gas use is brand new to the household. It helps explain the higher bill.

D is route two: price. If the utility raised its rates after the installation, Jimmy pays more for each unit of gas. The bill can rise even if the household burns less gas than before. D helps explain the increase, so eliminate it.

E is route one through heating. Unusually cold weather after the installation led to heavy gas usage. That extra gas has nothing to do with the water heater's efficiency, and it raises the bill. E helps explain the increase.

note: Goal claimed the efficient heater 'cannot explain a higher bill', which is false (a heater that underperforms its rating could); softened to a reason grounded in the stimulus.

steps.label: Given that ...
steps.body: Consumer demand for personal computers continues to increase each year.

steps.label: Why is it that ...
steps.body: The retail profit margin on personal computer sales is extremely low compared to that of other high-tech items.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Notice what the stimulus measures: the retail profit margin, meaning how much profit stores keep out of what they take in on PC sales. Rising demand might make us expect fat margins, since stores could charge more and still find buyers. But demand is only one input. A margin depends on the price the store charges and on what it costs the store to make each sale.

So there are two routes to a thin margin.

Price is held down: heavy competition, or stores choosing to keep PC prices low on purpose.

Costs are pushed up: expenses that come with selling PCs in particular, such as extra staff time or stock that loses value.

The stimulus also compares PCs with other popular high-tech items, so the strongest explanations hit PCs harder than those items.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: We need to find four reasons why PC's have a lower profit margin (or why other popular high-tech items have a higher profit margin). Each one should either lower what stores can charge for PCs or raise what it costs stores to sell them. The exception will do neither. Watch for an answer that is about PCs and their buyers but never touches the store's price or cost.

notes.body: A is the cost route. When computer technology changes fast, unsold stock is more likely to become obsolete. Obsolete stock gets marked down or written off, and that loss comes out of the store's profit on PC sales. A helps explain the thin margin, so eliminate it.

B is the exception. Brand loyalty is loyalty to a maker's brand, not to a store. Run the two-route test. Does B lower the price a store can charge? No. Does it raise what the store spends to make a sale? No. B also never compares PCs with the other high-tech items, so it gives no reason the PC margin in particular should be low.

C is the cost route, with the comparison built in. If PC buyers need more help from store employees than buyers of other high-tech items, each PC sale costs the store more in staff time. Higher cost per sale means a lower margin, and it explains the gap with other high-tech items too.

D is the price route, chosen on purpose. Stores keep PC prices low to bring in customers who might buy software and accessories. The PC works as a loss leader: the store accepts a thin margin on the computer to make money on the extras. That explains the low PC margin directly.

E is the price route through competition. More discount outlets selling PCs means more stores fighting for the same customers, and that fight is usually won on price. Lower prices squeeze margins even while demand keeps rising. E helps explain the discrepancy.

note: Writer-flagged B inference (loyal customers are easier to sell to, so better margins) is speculative and arguable either way; replaced with the missing comparison to other high-tech items.
D correctly shown to explain the repressing rather than the advantages; C quote now exact bank wording, replacing the old self-control misquote.

steps.label: Original Argument
steps.body:
Premise: People who have never been asked to do more than they can easily do never do all they can.
(Never pushed → never does all they can.)
Premise: Alex has not done all that Alex is capable of doing.
Conclusion: No one has ever pushed Alex to do more than what comes easily.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The flaw is affirming the consequent, also called mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one. The rule says: never pushed → does not do all they can. The argument sees the right side (Alex is not doing all Alex can) and concludes the left side (Alex was never pushed).

But the rule only runs one way. Someone who was pushed hard might still fall short: laziness, illness, bad luck. Falling short is necessary for being never pushed (everyone never pushed falls short), but it is not sufficient to prove it. The argument treats Alex falling short as enough to prove Alex was never pushed.

In plain shape:
All A are B.
X is B.
So X is A.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Find an answer with the same shape: a rule (A → B), a fact that something has B, and a conclusion that it has A.

For each answer, diagram the rule, then ask two questions. Does the evidence land on the rule's right side? Does the conclusion land on its left side? Expect two kinds of traps: an answer that negates the left side instead (a different flaw), and an answer that runs a valid contrapositive (no flaw at all).

notes.body:
A matches piece for piece. Rule: has a dog → knows the true value of companionship. Fact: Alicia has demonstrated knowing the true value of companionship, the right side. Conclusion: Alicia has a dog, the left side. That is the original's reversal exactly: observe the result, conclude the trigger. Alicia might value companionship because of friends, family or a cat.

The move to repeat: on a conditional parallel flaw question, diagram the rule, then check that the evidence and the conclusion land on the same sides of the arrow as in the original.

B diagrams as discovers something new → examined all possible solutions. Fran never discovered something new, which negates the left side, and the conclusion negates the right side. That is denying the trigger: a flaw, but not the original's, which affirmed the result. B also slides from examined to explored.

C is the topic lure: challenges and accomplishing everything sound like the original. Diagram it. Not sufficient challenges → does not accomplish everything one can. Jill accomplishes everything, which negates the right side, so Jill faces sufficient challenges, the negated left side. That is a valid contrapositive, and a parallel flaw answer has to be flawed.

D starts from a definition, and a definition runs both ways: every polygon is a closed plane figure bounded by straight lines, and every such figure is a polygon. So moving from the description to the label is valid. A large number of straight lines is still straight lines. There is no flaw here to match.

E is the closest trap, because it also seems to move from a result to a trigger. But the pieces do not line up. The rule's result is being lax about keeping property secure; the evidence shows Jon lax about property Jon can afford to lose, a narrower claim. The rule's trigger is never having lost something one cannot afford to lose; the conclusion is that Jon never lost anything at all. Both pieces drift from the rule's terms, so E is not the clean reversal the original makes. A copies it exactly.

note: E note said Jon is lax 'only' about affordable property, which E does not say; removed 'only'.
Correlation-to-advice recipe correctly matched in A; B, D, E correctly shown to have causal evidence and C a different flaw; new Goal row is additive.
